---
title: "Small multiples"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8.8, fig.height = 4.4, dpi = 100,
  fig.retina = 2, dev = "ragg_png", out.width = "100%"
)
options(gglaplot2.font = "inter")
library(ggplot2)
library(gglaplot2)
gbp <- label_gla_pounds(short = TRUE)
```

Three series on one chart is the design ceiling. Past it, or when the
series are on different scales, the web charts stack one panel per series
in a single column, each a full chart with its own axes and the series name
as its heading. `facet_gla_rows()` is that layout: `facet_wrap()` in one
column with the axes on every panel.

## Stacked panels

Colour each panel by its own series and drop the legend, since the headings
carry the names.

```{r rows, fig.height = 7}
ggplot(gla_monthly, aes(month, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_gla_line() +
  facet_gla_rows(vars(series)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = gbp) +
  scale_colour_gla() +
  gla_labs(title = "Each variable on its own", subtitle = "Monthly value, GBP",
           source = "LDN Viz Tools demo data", x = NULL) +
  theme_gla(legend = "none")
```

## Shared or free scales

The web chart gives each panel its own y range, which is what
`facet_gla_rows()` does by default. That shows the shape of each series
but hides their size against one another: a 5% movement looks the same as
a 50% one. When the panels are the same measure at a similar size, share
the scales with `scales = "fixed"` so the eye can compare heights.

```{r fixed, fig.height = 7}
ggplot(gla_monthly, aes(month, value, colour = series)) +
  geom_gla_line() +
  facet_gla_rows(vars(series), scales = "fixed") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = gla_breaks(), labels = gbp) +
  scale_colour_gla() +
  gla_labs(title = "The same, on one scale", subtitle = "Monthly value, GBP",
           source = "LDN Viz Tools demo data", x = NULL) +
  theme_gla(legend = "none")
```

## A grid

For panels that are not a single series each, ggplot2's own facets work
under `theme_gla()`: the strip takes the axis title role and sits left
over its panel. Bars and histograms facet the same way; the bar charts and
histograms articles each have an example.

```{r grid, fig.height = 4.4}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_gla_dot(size = 2.5) +
  facet_wrap(vars(cyl), labeller = label_both) +
  gla_labs(title = "Fuel economy by cylinders", subtitle = "Weight against miles per gallon",
           x = "Weight (1,000 lb)", y = "Miles per gallon") +
  theme_gla(gridlines = "both", axis_titles = "both")
```

## Interactive

`gla_plotly()` turns the finished chart into an interactive one through
plotly. Stacked panels convert with their strips and a y axis on every
panel.

```{r interactive, eval = requireNamespace("plotly", quietly = TRUE)}
gla_plotly(last_plot())
```
